rationale: Job's oath names the Almighty as the one who embittered him; his later complaint likewise directly attributes merciless treatment to God. These remain Job's descriptions of his suffering.
Job speaks of divine spirit remaining in his nostrils while he lives; Elihu describes the converse, all flesh dying if God retains the spirit with Himself.
Job promises that his lips will not speak lawlessness; the earlier narrator had specifically said he did not sin with his lips amid his affliction.
Job refuses to abandon his innocence despite his friends; the earlier divine speech explicitly says that he still holds to innocence. The speakers and settings remain distinct.
Job's refusal to relinquish righteousness is restated through the later appeal to a righteous balance and the Lord's knowledge of his innocence.
Job questions the ungodly person's hope, while Bildad had declared that the ungodly person's hope will perish. The comparison does not endorse Bildad's application to Job.

Job asks whether the Lord hears the ungodly person's plea in distress. Elihu later speaks of oppressed people crying out and of cries not heard because of evil people's insolence. The comparison concerns the lack of a hearing without identifying the oppressed criers with the ungodly person in Job's question.
Job questions the ungodly person's access and being heard before God; the proverb contrasts God's distance from the impious with His hearing righteous prayers.
Job accuses his hearers of piling emptiness upon emptiness, renewing his earlier rejection of their empty consolation.
Job's statement about an ungodly person's portion from the Lord closely repeats the formula that closes Zophar's speech. The shared formula does not equate their entire arguments.

Job here describes the ungodly person's sons facing slaughter and need; his earlier speech described ungodly people with children before their eyes and at play. Both descriptions are preserved without harmonizing their scope.
The silver and gold accumulated in Job's example belong to a sequence ending in transfer to the righteous; Ecclesiastes similarly describes a sinner gathering to give to someone good before God.
Job says righteous and truthful people will possess the accumulated money; the proverb expressly says the impious person's wealth is stored up for the righteous.
Job compares the ungodly person's house to moths and a spider; Bildad had compared the same kind of person's tent to a spider's web and said the house would not stand.
Job's rich man opens his eyes and is no more; Zophar's supposedly established man vanishes and is no longer seen in his place. No particular rich individual is identified.
The scorching wind winnows the ungodly man from his place, corresponding to Job's earlier image of such people as straw or dust swept away by wind.
The divine action against rock overturns mountains from their roots, recalling Job's earlier description of God overturning mountains. The descriptions are not assigned to a particular earthquake.

The uncovering of river depths and display of divine power in light recalls Job's earlier language of God uncovering deep things from darkness and bringing death's shadow into light; the objects uncovered remain distinct.
The question about wisdom's location receives the chapter's answer: God knows its way and place, and tells a human that reverence and abstaining from evil constitute wisdom and knowledge.
Job denies that treasure or weighed silver can purchase wisdom; Proverbs likewise places wisdom above gold, silver and costly stones.
Job excludes Ophir gold, onyx and sappheiros as wisdom's equivalent; Wisdom's speech likewise ranks knowledge and wisdom above gold and costly stones, without identifying each named stone.
Job denies that gold, glass or golden vessels can equal wisdom; Proverbs says neither gold and silver nor anything precious is worthy of her. The comparison does not supply glass to Proverbs.
Job says Ethiopian topazion and pure gold cannot equal wisdom; the proverb similarly says wisdom exceeds costly stones and every precious thing, without equating particular gemstones.

Wisdom is hidden from humans and heaven's birds, whereas the subsequent statement explicitly says God knows its place. This preserves the chapter's contrast between creaturely limits and divine knowledge.

relationship: Divine possession and gift of wisdom
rationale: Job places knowledge of wisdom's way and place with God; Proverbs names the Lord as the giver of wisdom, knowledge and understanding.
Job names the weight of winds and measures of water; Isaiah's question similarly depicts God measuring waters and weighing features of creation. The measured objects are not made identical.

The statement that God counted rain and a path for sounds amid a shaking is compared with the Lord's later question about preparing violent rain's flow and a path for tumult. The unusual wording is retained.

relationship: Wisdom and the ordering of creation
rationale: Job describes God seeing, expounding and preparing wisdom in the account of ordering the world; Proverbs presents Wisdom with the Lord before and during His works. No identity of every temporal expression is asserted.
Job's statement that reverence for God is wisdom corresponds directly to the proverb that fear of the Lord is wisdom's beginning.
Job joins reverence for God to abstaining from evils; the proverb explicitly says that through fear of the Lord everyone turns from evil.
Job longs for the former days when God guarded him; the prologue's speech about God's fence around Job and his household supplies the earlier depiction of protection.

Job remembers walking through darkness by God's light; Eliphaz had promised brightness upon his ways as part of restoration. The comparison distinguishes Job's recollection from Eliphaz's conditional counsel.
Job remembers his children around him in prosperous days; the opening account identifies his sons and daughters and their shared meals before the losses.

Job pictures his former roads and mountains flooded with butter and milk; Zophar had wished that the ungodly person not see the milking of herds or pastures of honey and butter. The figurative and stated details are preserved.
Young men once hid and elders stood when Job appeared; the next speech describes laughter and admonition from those he calls the least. The groups are not assumed to be identical people.

Job recalls powerful men's respectful silence, in contrast with the later admonition he receives from the least. The comparison concerns the reversal in his treatment, not an identification of the two groups.

Job claims to have rescued a poor person and helped an orphan; Eliphaz had accused him of withholding aid and mistreating orphans. These are opposed claims in the debate, not two proven accounts of wrongdoing.
Job recalls a widow blessing him, directly contrasting with Eliphaz's accusation that he sent widows away empty.

Job describes clothing himself with righteousness and wrapping himself in justice; Isaiah depicts the Lord putting on righteousness as a breastplate and wrapping Himself in garments. The wearers and garments remain distinct.
Job's claim to have been a father to the powerless is developed in his later oath about sharing food with an orphan and nourishing like a father.
Job recalls expecting a long life; the ending later reports his extended years, descendants and death full of days. His palm-trunk comparison is not turned into a numerical prediction.
Job's image of a root open toward water and a harvest receiving dew is compared with Jeremiah's trusting person portrayed as a tree sending roots toward moisture and continuing to bear fruit.

relationship: Formerly heeded counsel and present rebuke
rationale: Job remembers others keeping silent at his counsel; his ensuing account instead has the least taking turns admonishing him. The contrast preserves the change in his social position.
Job says his hearers awaited his speech like thirsty earth awaiting rain; the song in Deuteronomy asks that its utterance be awaited as rain and descend as dew.

Job recalls sitting among people in the manner of one consoling sufferers; the narrative instead presents his three friends coming to comfort him in his affliction. The comparison concerns his changed role.
The present laughter and admonition are set against Job's immediately preceding account of young men hiding and elders standing before him. No identity of particular observers is claimed.
Job says his detractors have him as their repeated tale and lyre; he earlier described being made a tale among nations and a laughingstock.
The present group's abhorrence and distancing repeat the rejection Job earlier reported from those who had known and loved him. The two groups are not equated.
Job says God opened His quiver and mistreated him; his earlier complaint located the Lord's arrows in his body. Both remain Job's descriptions of affliction.
Job says God stripped off his robe; his earlier complaint likewise described God stripping away his glory and removing his crown. The garments and symbols are not conflated.
Job's complaint about divine missiles corresponds with his earlier description of being set up as a target and surrounded by spears. Neither passage establishes a literal human battle.
Job says hope went away like wind and salvation like a cloud; he earlier described life perishing in empty hope and disappearance like a cloud cleared from heaven.
Job's burned bones and disjoined sinews at night develop his earlier complaint that nights of pain and suffering from evening to morning had been allotted to him.
Job says God regards him as clay and describes his portion as earth and ashes; his earlier appeal recalled being molded as clay and turned back to earth.

relationship: Earth and ashes in distinct settings
rationale: The phrase earth and ashes reappears when Job responds after the Lord's speech. The earlier complaint about his condition and the later self-description are preserved as different settings.

relationship: Unanswered appeal and later divine speech
rationale: Job complains that he cries to God without being heard; the narrative later records the Lord speaking to Job after Elihu has ceased. This identifies the eventual speech without claiming every complaint receives a specific answer.
Job's charge of merciless scourging recalls his earlier description of being torn apart and struck without sparing. The accusations are attributed to Job.
Job calls earth the house of every mortal; Genesis states that the human will return to the earth from which he was taken.

Job's recollection of weeping for the powerless and constrained is compared with his earlier account of rescuing the poor and receiving a widow's blessing; it supplies the moral setting of his lament.
Job's expectation of good followed by days of evil contrasts with his earlier recollection of expecting to grow old and live long.

Job names himself a brother to sirens and companion to ostriches; Micah pictures lamentation like dragons and mourning like daughters of sirens. The shared lament imagery does not equate the creature lists.

relationship: Physical affliction in narrative and lament
rationale: Job describes his darkened skin and scorched bones after the narrative has reported the grievous ulcer from feet to head. The comparison connects the continuing affliction without diagnosing its medical cause.
Job's lyre and song become suffering and weeping; Amos likewise announces songs turning into lamentation. The separate speakers and circumstances are not identified as the same event.
Job's covenant concerning his eyes and attention toward a virgin is compared with Jesus' warning about looking at a woman to lust after her. The different formulations and audiences are preserved.
Job asks whether destruction belongs to the unjust, recalling his earlier announcement of the ungodly person's portion from the Lord.
Job asks whether God sees his way and counts his steps; Elihu later asserts that God observes human works and that nothing they do escapes Him.
Job asks for a righteous weighing because the Lord knows his innocence; he earlier insisted that he would hold to righteousness and was not conscious of improper acts.

Job's oath includes the possibility of his heart following his eye; Proverbs warns against being hunted by one's own eyes in the context of desire. The additional road and gift clauses in Job are not supplied to Proverbs.

relationship: Harvest consumed by others as a curse
rationale: Job conditionally calls for others to eat what he sows; Deuteronomy's curse likewise has another nation consume the land's yield and labor. This is a comparison of curse forms, not proof Job incurred the covenant curse.
Job's oath denies pursuing another man's wife and waiting at her doors; Proverbs warns that one who goes in to a married woman will not be acquitted.
Job's conditional self-curse concerning his wife and children is compared with the covenant curse of taking a wife whom another man will have. The distinct wording about children is not harmonized.
Job describes defiling a man's wife as an unrestrainable fury of wrath; Proverbs describes the husband's jealous anger and refusal to spare.
The fire burning through every part continues Job's description of adultery; Proverbs likewise uses carrying fire and walking on coals to explain the danger of approaching a married woman.

relationship: Impartial hearing of a subordinate's case
rationale: Job's oath concerns not despising a servant's case against him; Deuteronomy commands just hearings without favoring the great over the small. The people named in the two passages remain distinct.
Job asks what answer he could give if God inspected his treatment of servants; he had similarly warned his friends that God's examination would expose partiality rather than excuse it.
Job grounds his treatment of servants in their formation just like his own; the proverb says that the Lord made both rich and poor. Neither passage erases the distinct social descriptions.

relationship: Denial opposed to treatment of widows
rationale: Job denies letting a widow's eye waste away or leaving the powerless without their need; Eliphaz had accused him of sending widows away empty.

relationship: Sharing food versus accusation of withholding
rationale: Job's oath includes not eating alone without sharing with an orphan; Eliphaz had accused him of depriving the hungry of a morsel. These opposed claims remain attributed to their speakers.
The claim of nourishing like a father, following the orphan clause, recalls Job's earlier description of being a father to the powerless.

relationship: Clothing the naked versus accusation of stripping
rationale: Job's oath denies disregarding a naked person without clothing him; Eliphaz had accused him of taking away the naked person's clothing.
Job describes the powerless blessing him for warmth from his lambs' wool; his earlier recollection likewise includes a widow's blessing. The recipients are not identified as the same people.
Job's oath denies raising a hand against an orphan despite available help; Eliphaz's earlier accusation expressly charged him with mistreating orphans.

relationship: Fear of God and avoidance of wrongdoing
rationale: Job names fear of the Lord as gripping him within his oath against injustice; the wisdom conclusion likewise joins reverence for God with abstaining from evils.
Job's oath rejects appointing gold as his strength or trusting a costly stone; Proverbs warns that the one who trusts wealth will fall.

relationship: Not rejoicing at an enemy's fall
rationale: Job's oath denies rejoicing at his enemies' fall; Proverbs directly commands against rejoicing when an enemy falls or trips.
Job says a stranger did not lodge outside and his door stood open; Lot urges visitors to lodge in his house when they propose sleeping in the square. The guests and incidents are not equated.
Job's conditional oath addresses hiding an unintentional sin; Proverbs says one who covers his own impiety will not prosper. Job's unintentional qualification is preserved.

relationship: Not dismissing a powerless person empty
rationale: The final clause of Job's oath concerns sending the powerless away with an empty fold; Deuteronomy commands opening the hand to a needy brother and supplying his need. The separate confession clause is not merged with this comparison.

In the written-bond sequence, Job describes tearing it up and returning it while taking nothing from the debtor; Deuteronomy commands release rather than exacting a brother's debt. Job's bond is not recast as an indictment against God.

relationship: Uncompensated use of the land's produce
rationale: Job's oath addresses consuming the land's strength without payment and harming its owner; his earlier account described work in others' fields and vineyards without pay or food. The injured landowner and exploited workers remain distinct.
Job conditionally calls for nettles and bramble instead of wheat and barley; Genesis' curse has the earth bring thorns and thistles. The plant lists and circumstances are not identified as identical.

relationship: Narrative evaluation of Job and the friends
rationale: The narrator says the friends stopped contradicting Job because he was righteous before them; the ending gives the Lord's separate rebuke that the three had not spoken truth as Job had. This does not make the two judgments identical in wording or authority.

relationship: Elihu's response to Job's righteousness claim
rationale: Elihu's anger is tied to Job declaring himself righteous before the Lord; Job's own earlier statement explicitly maintains his righteousness and innocence. Elihu's characterization remains distinct from Job's words.

relationship: Different censures of the three friends
rationale: Elihu is angry that the friends could not answer Job and declared him ungodly; the Lord later rebukes them for not speaking truth concerning Job. The different grounds of censure are preserved, without making the Lord endorse Elihu.

relationship: Same-chapter narrated reason and speaker's explanation
rationale: The narrator says Elihu waited because the others were older; Elihu then explains that his own youth and their age had made him keep quiet.
Elihu reports his prior thought that time and many years bring wisdom, echoing Job's earlier saying that wisdom and knowledge accompany much time and long life.
Elihu's general claim that the Almighty's breath teaches mortals is repeated in his personal statement that the same breath teaches him. The latter also says divine spirit made him.

relationship: Challenge to age as a guarantee of wisdom
rationale: Elihu denies that the long-lived are wise or elders know judgment, in tension with Job's earlier association of long life with wisdom. His preceding recollection and appeal to divine breath supply the setting of the challenge.

relationship: Claiming attachment to God does not establish wisdom
rationale: Elihu warns the friends not to say that they found wisdom by attaching themselves to the Lord; Job had warned that attaching themselves to Him would not prevent divine reproof for partiality.

relationship: Same-chapter pressure to speak and intended relief
rationale: Elihu describes being full of words and distressed by the spirit of his belly, then states that he will speak so that he may rest. The comparison follows the expressed pressure and intended relief.

Elihu's tied wineskin contains fermenting new wine as an image of his pressure to speak, and his separate bellows image explicitly bursts; Jesus describes new wine bursting old wineskins. The vessels and uses are kept distinct.

relationship: Not shrinking before a human in judgment
rationale: Elihu promises not to be overawed by a mortal; the judicial instruction similarly says not to shrink before a human face because judgment belongs to God.
Elihu says he does not know how to show partiality; Deuteronomy expressly requires judging the small and great alike without partiality. Elihu's additional moth warning is not supplied to the law.
Elihu claims purity of heart and lips in his speech, as Job had promised that his lips and soul would not speak or devise lawlessness. These remain the respective speakers' claims.

relationship: Personal application of divine teaching by breath
rationale: Elihu applies to himself his prior statement about the Almighty's breath teaching mortals; he also attributes his making to divine spirit. Breath is not silently changed from teaching to a different action.

relationship: Invitation to contend in the debate
rationale: Elihu invites Job to answer and stand against him; Job earlier asked who would enter judgment with him. This compares the expressed challenges without identifying Elihu with God.
Elihu stresses that he and Job were fashioned from the same clay, recalling Job's own statement that God molded him as clay.

relationship: Reassurance about fear and a heavy hand
rationale: Elihu says his fear will not overwhelm Job and his hand will not be heavy; Job had asked God to keep His hand away and not overwhelm him with terror. Elihu remains a human interlocutor.

relationship: Reported innocence compared with Job's own claim
rationale: Elihu represents Job as claiming to be clean and blameless; Job's earlier speech supplies his own assertion of righteousness and lack of consciousness of improper deeds. This is not treated as an exact quotation of every clause.
Elihu reports Job's claim that God regards him as an opponent; Job had expressly said that God regarded him like an enemy.
Elihu's report of a foot in a wooden restraint and guarded ways closely echoes Job's own complaint about his foot in a restraint and all his works being watched.

relationship: Reported complaint of not being heard
rationale: Elihu challenges the claim that God has not heard Job; Job had directly complained that he cried to God and was not heard. Elihu's additional framing of righteousness remains his own.

relationship: Desire to present a case and receive an answer
rationale: Elihu represents Job as asking why his case was not heard; Job earlier described wanting to state his case and understand God's reply. The report and the earlier expression of desire remain distinct.

relationship: Divine communication in a nocturnal experience
rationale: Elihu introduces speech through a dream or nighttime meditation; Eliphaz's earlier account contains nighttime terror, a spirit and a heard voice. No identity between the experiences is asserted.

Elihu describes fearful nighttime experiences upon a bed; Job had complained that instead of his bed comforting him, God frightened him with dreams and visions. Elihu's interpretation is not imposed as a proven explanation of Job's dreams.

relationship: Warning that turns a person from a wrong course
rationale: Elihu describes divine warning intended to turn a human from injustice; the angel's confrontation leads Balaam to acknowledge sin and offer to turn back. The dream and road encounter remain different settings.

Elihu presents weakness on a bed as divine reproof; Eliphaz had likewise joined the Lord's correction with wounding and healing. Their interpretation is attributed to the speakers rather than established as Job's particular guilt.

relationship: Affliction and inability to receive food
rationale: Elihu's generic sufferer cannot receive food despite desire; Job earlier described his food as a stench. The comparison identifies similar distress without proving Elihu's explanation of its cause.
Elihu's illustrative sufferer loses flesh and shows bones, recalling Job's description of his flesh decaying within his skin and his bones. The illustrative human is not declared to be Job.
The illustrative human draws near death; in the ensuing conditional account God holds him back from falling into death and renews his body. The stated conditions are not removed.
Elihu's conditional bodily renewal and preservation from death correspond to Eliphaz's description of the God who causes pain and then restores. Neither saying establishes Job's guilt.

relationship: Restored flesh compared with a child's
rationale: Elihu describes flesh softened like an infant's; Naaman's flesh is restored like that of a little child. This compares the restoration image without identifying the sufferer or the means of healing.

relationship: Turning toward God and accepted prayer
rationale: Elihu's sequence of turning, confession and accepted prayer is compared with Eliphaz's sequence of returning to the Lord and having prayer heard. Both are the speakers' presentations of restoration.

relationship: Not dealt with according to sins
rationale: The restored person says he was not examined as his sins deserved; the psalm likewise says God has not dealt with His people according to their sins or lawless deeds.

relationship: Same-chapter plea and repeated deliverance language
rationale: The plea for rescue from corruption and life seeing light is followed by Elihu's first-person statement of rescue from death to praise in light. The change of voice is preserved rather than identifying both speakers.

relationship: Rescue from death and life in light
rationale: Elihu speaks of his soul being rescued from death to praise God in light; the psalm links rescue from death with being pleasing before God in the light of the living.
Elihu says he wants Job to be justified and invites him to answer; Job had expressed confidence that he would be shown righteous. Elihu's expressed aim is distinguished from his later accusations.

relationship: Repeated test of words and food
rationale: Elihu repeats the distinctive comparison Job used earlier: the ear tests or discerns words as the throat tastes food.

relationship: Elihu's summary and Job's actual speech
rationale: Elihu summarizes Job as righteous yet deprived of judgment; Job's speech joins his complaint about God's treatment with his insistence on innocence. The summary is not treated as an exact quotation of the full passage.

relationship: Violent arrow in the report of Job's complaint
rationale: Elihu's reported violent arrow recalls Job's own description of the Lord's arrows in his body. The added statement about judgment is not silently supplied to the earlier text.

relationship: Shared drinking metaphor: mockery and injustice
rationale: Elihu pictures Job drinking mockery like water; Eliphaz had pictured an unclean man drinking injustice as a drink. The comparison concerns the drinking image and preserves its different objects; the following Job 34:8 says without sinning or acting ungodly, so drinking mockery is not silently treated as the same wrongdoing as drinking injustice.

relationship: Divine inspection asserted against a question
rationale: Elihu rejects saying there will be no divine inspection; Job had asked why God had not inspected the oppression described in his speech. The asserted answer does not erase the earlier question.
Elihu says God repays each human according to action and path; Jeremiah likewise speaks of the Lord giving each according to ways and the fruits of practices.
Elihu's question whether the Lord will do improper things or disturb judgment closely parallels Bildad's question whether the Lord will do wrong in judging or disturb what is right.
Elihu considers God retaining the spirit with Himself, leading to universal death; the psalm describes God taking back creatures' breath so that they fail and return to dust.

relationship: Mortals returning to their source earth
rationale: Elihu says every mortal returns to the earth from which he was formed; Genesis directly states the human's return to the earth from which he was taken.

Elihu calls the person who labels a king or ruler lawless ungodly; the command in Exodus forbids speaking evil of the people's rulers. This compares the speech restriction without making Elihu's entire political argument divine narration.

relationship: Those who turn aside the weak not receiving help
rationale: Elihu describes lawless people whose requests for human help prove empty after the powerless were turned aside; the proverb similarly links blocking the weak person's cry with one's own call going unheard.
Elihu asserts that God observes human works without missing any; Job had asked whether God sees his way and counts all his steps.
Elihu denies a hiding place to those doing lawless things; the Lord's question in Jeremiah likewise denies that a person can hide where He cannot see.
Elihu's description of unsearchable, glorious and terrible things beyond number recalls Job's earlier description of God's great, unsearchable and extraordinary deeds beyond numbering.

relationship: Hearing the oppressed poor person's cry
rationale: Elihu says God hears the needy and poor person's cry arising from oppression; Exodus warns about retaining a neighbor's covering and says God will hear that person's cry because He is merciful.

Elihu says a hypocritical human is made king because of a people's perversity; Hosea says a king was given in divine anger in the setting of Israel's injustice. No particular king in Job is identified with Israel's king.

The proposed appeal asks God to show the speaker and promises not to add to injustice if he practiced it; Job had asked to be taught his sins and lawless deeds. The comparison does not replace apart from myself I will see with a claim of not having seen.

relationship: Elihu's repeated accusation of ignorant speech
rationale: The charge that Job's words lack knowledge is repeated in Elihu's later accusation that Job opens his mouth vainly and weighs down words in ignorance. It remains Elihu's accusation.
Elihu warns that speaking many words before the Lord may add to sins and incur lawlessness; Proverbs similarly warns that much talking does not escape sin. The collective wording in Job is preserved.
